title: Judah's Pledge and the Feast in Joseph's House
summary: When the grain runs out, Judah persuades Jacob to let Benjamin go to Egypt by pledging his own life for the boy's safety. The brothers return with gifts and double silver, fear a trap when they are brought to Joseph's house, and are released from their fear by the steward, who restores Simeon to them. Joseph, overcome at the sight of Benjamin, weeps in private, then seats the brothers in order of age and gives Benjamin a portion five times larger than the rest.
story: The famine does not relent, and Jacob's refusal at the end of Genesis 42 cannot last. What changes the deadlock is Judah. This is the brother who proposed selling Joseph for silver (37:26-27) and who was later humbled by Tamar (Genesis 38). Reuben's offer to let his own sons be killed was rejected; Judah's offer is different, because he puts himself on the line: “I will guarantee his safety.” For the first time a son of Leah takes personal responsibility for a son of Rachel. Jacob yields with a prayer and a heavy resignation, and the scene moves to Egypt, where fear turns into an unexpected feast. The chapter ends in apparent peace, the brothers eating and drinking with the man they still do not recognize, but the final and hardest test is about to begin in Genesis 44.
historical:
The famine is now in its second year (45:6), and grain from Egypt is the only thing standing between Jacob's household and starvation. Jacob's gift for the Egyptian official is made of the best products of the land: balm, honey, spices, myrrh, pistachios, and almonds. These were the kinds of goods that caravans carried from Canaan down to Egypt, and they echo the cargo of the traders who carried Joseph there as a slave: “spices, balm, and myrrh” (37:25). The brothers also carry double silver, to repay what they found in their sacks and to buy again.

Joseph's household runs as an Egyptian official's would. He has a steward over his house, a position well attested in Egyptian records, who handles guests, money, and meals, and the brothers are brought to dine at noon. Joseph eats apart from both his brothers and his Egyptian guests. The narrator explains that the Egyptians would not eat with Hebrews, and the Greek historian Herodotus, writing in the fifth century BC, reported a similar reluctance among Egyptians to share cooking vessels or knives with Greeks. Joseph's separate table also reflects his rank.
cultural:
The chapter is full of the customs of hospitality and honor. Gifts smoothed the way before a powerful man, as when Jacob sent gifts ahead to Esau (32:13-21). The steward's water for washing feet and fodder for the donkeys were the marks of a proper welcome (compare 18:4 and 24:32). The brothers bow to the ground twice (vv. 26, 28), now eleven of them, as in Joseph's dream of eleven stars bowing (37:9).

The seating by birth order astonishes the brothers, since there was no way an Egyptian stranger should know their ages. Portions sent from the host's table were a sign of honor, and Benjamin's portion, five times larger than anyone else's, singles him out as the favored one. Many readers think Joseph is quietly testing whether the old jealousy that once turned the brothers against a favored son of Rachel is still alive. This time the text records no resentment. They feast and drink freely.
literary: The chapter has two halves. In Canaan (vv. 1-14) the argument is resolved by Judah's pledge and Jacob's prayer; in Egypt (vv. 15-34) the brothers' fear is resolved by grace they do not understand. The brothers expect punishment at every turn: they assume the invitation to Joseph's house is a trap (v. 18) and rush to explain the silver before anyone accuses them. The steward's reply is loaded with irony: “Your God, the God of your father, gave you the treasure that was in your sacks.” He says more than he knows. Joseph's weeping, the second of several such scenes (42:24; 45:2, 14-15; 50:17), marks the growing pressure of his love for his brothers against the role he is playing. The chapter builds toward calm (a meal, wine, honor) so that the shock of Genesis 44 will be all the greater.

outline.t: The grain runs out and Judah pledges himself for Benjamin
Jacob's gift, double silver, and prayer
The brothers' fear at Joseph's house and the steward's reassurance
Joseph sees Benjamin, weeps, and hosts the feast

doctrines.note: The steward's words, that the brothers' God had given them the treasure in their sacks, are true in a deeper sense than he intends. Behind the returned silver, the invitation, and the feast is a God who is working toward reconciliation while the brothers expect only judgment.

Jacob sends his sons with the only thing he can still give them: “May God Almighty grant you mercy before the man.” He uses the name God Almighty (El Shaddai), under which God had promised him a nation (35:11). His prayer is joined to honest grief, “if I am bereaved, I am bereaved”, and shows that surrender and petition can stand together.

Judah's pledge begins the healing of a family divided by favoritism. The father who loved one son above the others, and the brothers who hated that son, are being brought to a point where one brother will risk himself for another.

words.note: Arav, to stand surety or pledge oneself for another. In verse 9 Judah becomes the guarantor for Benjamin, accepting that if he fails he will bear the guilt all his life. Proverbs repeatedly warns against rashly standing surety for strangers (for example 6:1 and 11:15), which shows how serious such a pledge was. Judah will make good on it in 44:32-33.

Rachamim, compassion or tender mercy, a word related to the Hebrew for womb. Jacob prays that God will give his sons mercy before the man (v. 14), and in verse 30 the same word describes Joseph's feelings for Benjamin, literally that his compassion grew warm. The prayer is answered in the heart of the man it names.

To'evah, something detestable or abhorrent. The Egyptians regarded eating with Hebrews as detestable (v. 32), and in 46:34 shepherds are said to be detestable to them. In the law the word is used for practices God finds abhorrent, especially idolatry. Here it marks the social distance between Egypt and Jacob's family, which will help keep Israel a distinct people in Goshen.

christ: Judah's pledge is the chapter's clearest link to the larger story. Judah offers himself as the guarantor of his brother's life, and in the next chapter he will offer to become a slave in Benjamin's place. Jesus came from the tribe of Judah (Hebrews 7:14), and Hebrews calls him the guarantee of a better covenant (Hebrews 7:22), using a Greek word for one who stands surety for another. The connection is thematic rather than predictive, since Genesis does not present Judah's pledge as a prophecy, but it shows the pattern the gospel fulfills: one who binds himself to bear the consequences so that another may come home. Joseph's table also carries a hint of the gospel's surprise, as men who feared a trap find themselves welcomed and fed by the brother they wronged.

hard.q: Jacob and Judah call Benjamin a boy, but he seems to be a grown man with sons. Which is it?
hard.a:
Benjamin was born before Joseph was sold (35:16-18), and more than twenty years have passed, so he is an adult. The Hebrew word used for him, na'ar, has a wide range, from a newborn to a young man of fighting age; Joseph himself is called one at seventeen (37:2), and David uses it of his grown son Absalom (2 Samuel 18:5). In Jacob's mouth it also carries a father's protectiveness toward the last son of his beloved Rachel.

Genesis 46:21 lists ten sons of Benjamin among those who went down to Egypt. Some readers take this at face value and conclude that Benjamin already had a large family. Others note that Numbers 26:40 lists two of those names, Ard and Naaman, as grandsons of Benjamin rather than sons, and conclude that the list in Genesis 46 is arranged by clan and includes descendants born later in Egypt. Either way, the language of this chapter reflects the family's view of Benjamin as the youngest and most protected, not a claim that he was a child.

questions: Judah, who once sold his brother for silver, now pledges his own life for his brother. What does his change suggest about whether people can really change, and what brings it about?
Jacob prays for mercy and then says, “if I am bereaved, I am bereaved.” Is that faith, resignation, or both? When have you had to release something you could not protect?
The brothers were afraid of the very house where a feast was being prepared for them. Why can grace be harder to receive than judgment?
